The Thirteenth Amendment. The Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified in December eighteen sixty-five, abolished slavery throughout the United States and its territories. Authored by President Abraham Lincoln and championed through Congress during the final year of the American Civil War, the amendment represented the constitutional culmination of the anti-slavery movement and formally eradicated the institution that had defined American society for nearly three centuries.

Abraham Lincoln introduced the amendment as a war measure and moral imperative, framing abolition not merely as military necessity but as constitutional principle. Its passage required a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress. The amendment's language is stark: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction."

This exception clause permitting involuntary servitude as criminal punishment has had enormous consequences. It enabled convict leasing, chain gangs, and mass incarceration, which many scholars argue represents slavery's continuation under a different name. The amendment was ratified by twenty-seven of the then thirty-six states, with ratification completed in December eighteen sixty-five, just months after General Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox. Southern states were coerced into ratifying as a condition of Reconstruction.

The Thirteenth Amendment was the first constitutional amendment to restrict individual liberty rather than enlarging rights. It established the federal government's power to regulate labor and social conditions nationwide. The amendment's ratification did not end racial oppression. The subsequent Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, Reconstruction legislation, and later Civil Rights Act were necessary to address the legal and de facto discrimination that persisted despite formal abolition.
